title: Theorem
body_md: Let $\Lambda$ be an even lattice of discriminant $2p^2$ in a positive definite, ternary quadratic space $(V,Q)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. Then for each $k\geq 0$ and $d\in\{1,p\}$ there exists a Hecke-equivariant isomorphism (for the algebra generated by the Hecke operators $T_q$ with $q\neq p$ prime): \[\mathcal{S}(O(V), O(\widehat{\Lambda}),W_{2k}\otimes \theta_d) \cong S_{2k+2}^{\textup{new}}\left(\Gamma_0(p),\varepsilon^{(p)}_p\varepsilon^{(p)}_d\right).\]

label: OtoSO
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{OtoSO}
For each lattice $\Lambda\subset V$ there is a Hecke-equivariant isomorphism: \[\mathcal{M}(O(V), O(\widehat{\Lambda}),W_{2k}\otimes \theta_d) \cong M(SO(V),SO(\widehat{\Lambda}), W_{2k}\otimes \theta_d)\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The restriction map from $O(\widehat{V})$ to $SO(\widehat{V})$ induces a Hecke-equivariant injective homomorphism \[\mathcal{M}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Lambda}),W) \longrightarrow M(SO(V),SO(\widehat{\Lambda}),W)\] for any representation $W$ of $O(V)$. The image consists of functions \[\varphi\in M(SO(V),SO(\widehat{\Lambda}),W)\] such that $\varphi(g) = \varphi((-I)\cdot g) = (-I)\cdot \varphi(g)$ for every $g\in SO(\widehat{V})$. When $-I$ acts trivially on $W$ this condition is automatically satisfied and so we get a Hecke-equivariant isomorphism. All of the representations constructed above have this property, establishing the result.

label: thm: 6.12 in HTV
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm: 6.12 in HTV}
Suppose that $\Lambda\subset V$ is an even lattice in a positive definite ternary quadratic space $(V,Q)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. Suppose that the associated quaternion algebra $B = \textup{Cl}^0(V)$ has discriminant $D$ and that the order $\mathcal{O} = \textup{Cl}^0(\Lambda)$ is residually unramified everywhere of discriminant $N = \textup{discrd}(\mathcal{O}) = \frac{1}{2}\textup{disc}(\Lambda)$. Let $N^+$ and $N^-$ be the products of the prime powers $p^e||N$ that satisfy $\varepsilon_p(\mathcal{O}) = 1$ and $\varepsilon_p(\mathcal{O}) = -1$ respectively. 

Then for each $k \geq 0$ and each square-free $d\mid N$ we have a Hecke-equivariant isomorphism (for all Hecke operators $T_p$ with $p \nmid N$):
$$\mathcal{S}(O(V), O(\widehat{\Lambda}), W_{2k}\otimes \theta_d) \cong 
\bigoplus_{M|N^-} S_{2k+2}^{M\textup{-new}}(\Gamma_0(MN^{+}), \varepsilon_D^{(MN^{+})}\varepsilon_d^{(MN^{+})})$$
where the sum runs over $M|N^-$ with $v_p(M) \equiv v_p(N) \bmod 2$ for all primes $p \,|\, N^-$.

label: samespace
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{samespace}
Suppose $\Lambda,\Pi\subset V$ are lattices such that $O(\widehat{\Lambda}) = O(\widehat{\Pi})$. Then for each representation $W$ of $O(V)$ there is an equality of Hecke modules: \[\mathcal{M}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Lambda}),W) = \mathcal{M}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Pi}),W).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Since $O(\widehat{\Lambda}) = O(\widehat{\Pi})$ is follows that $\mathcal{M}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Lambda}),W) = \mathcal{M}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Pi}),W)$ as spaces. We also have that: \[O(\widehat{\Lambda})\,g\, O(\widehat{\Lambda}) = O(\widehat{\Pi})\,g\, O(\widehat{\Pi})\] for any $g\in O(\widehat{V})$. This implies that we get the same Hecke representatives and hence the same Hecke operators on both sides.
head: environment

label: scaling
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{scaling}
Let $\Lambda\subset V$ be a lattice in a quadratic space $(V,Q)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. The Hecke module $\mathcal{M}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Lambda}),W)$ is invariant under non-zero scaling of the underlying quadratic map $Q$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: This is also clear. For any $\alpha\in\mathbb{Q}^{\times}$ the scaled quadratic space $(V,Q^{(\alpha)})$ has the same orthogonal group as $(V,Q)$. The same is true for $(\widehat{V},Q^{(\alpha)})$ and $(\widehat{V},Q)$. Consequently, the subgroup $O(\widehat{\Lambda})$ is invariant under scaling of the underlying quadratic map, which by Lemma \ref{samespace} implies an equality of spaces of orthogonal modular forms and Hecke operators.

label: p-mod
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{p-mod}
Let $p$ be an odd prime. Suppose that $(V_p,Q)$ is a ternary quadratic space over $\mathbb{Q}_p$ containing a $p$-adic lattice $\Lambda_p\subset V_p$ with Gram matrix $\langle a,p,pb\rangle$ for some $a,b\in\{1,r\}$. Then the $p$-adic sublattice $\Pi_p\subset V_p$ of index $p$ with Gram matrix $\langle p^2a,p,pb\rangle$ satisfies $O(\Lambda_p) = O(\Pi_p)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Theorem $1.1(2)$ of Allcock \cite{allcock2025} shows that $O(\Lambda_2)$ is maximal in $O(V_2)$ among the orthogonal groups of all $2$-adic lattices. Hence it again suffices to show that $O(\Lambda_2) \subseteq O(\Pi_2)$.

Fix a basis $\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}$ for $\Lambda_2$ realising the Gram matrix above. The $2^2+2+1 = 7$ sublattices of $\Lambda_2$ of index $2$ then have bases: \[\{2v_1,v_2,v_3\} \qquad \{v_1+\alpha v_2,2v_2,v_3\}\qquad \{v_1+\alpha v_3, v_2 + \beta v_3, 2v_3\}\] with $\alpha,\beta\in\{0,1\}$ and corresponding Gram matrices:

\[\begin{pmatrix}
4a & 0 & 0\\ 0 & b & 0\\ 0 & 0 & c
\end{pmatrix}\qquad \begin{pmatrix}
a+b\alpha^2 & 2b\alpha & 0\\ 2b\alpha & 4b & 0\\ 0 & 0 & c
\end{pmatrix} \qquad \begin{pmatrix}
a+c\alpha^2 & c\alpha\beta & 2c
\alpha\\ c\alpha\beta & b+c\beta^2 & 2c\beta\\ 2c\alpha & 2c\beta & 4c
\end{pmatrix}.\]

Note that $\Pi_2$ is the sublattice with Gram matrix corresponding to the choice $\alpha=\beta = 1$. It is also the only sublattice having norm ideal $\mathbb{Z}_2$ (the rest give norm ideal $\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}_2$). A similar argument to before shows that $O(\Lambda_2)\subseteq O(\Pi_2)$, as required.

It remains to show the equivalence of Gram matrices.  First we notice that: \[\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 1 & 0\\ -\frac{2bc}{\Delta} & -\frac{2ac}{\Delta} & 1\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
a+c & c & 2c
\\ c & b+c & 2c\\ 2c & 2c & 4c
\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & -\frac{2bc}{\Delta}\\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{2ac}{\Delta}\\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}a+c & c & 0\\ c & b+c & 0\\ 0 & 0 & \frac{4abc}{\Delta}\end{pmatrix}\] (noting that $\Delta\in\mathbb{Z}_2^{\times}$ since $a,b,c\in\{1,3,5,7\}$). The rest then follows by realising that the top left $2\times 2$ block is unimodular of type II with determinant $\Delta$, so must be equivalent to $\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ when $\Delta \equiv 7 \bmod 8$ or $\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ when $\Delta \equiv 3 \bmod 8$ (Theorem $8.9$ of \cite{gerstein2008basic}).

label: genus1
title: Theorem
body_md: \label{genus1} Let $\Lambda$ be a lattice representing Genus $1$. Then for each $k\geq 0$ and $d\in\{1,p\}$ there exists a Hecke-equivariant isomorphism (for the algebra generated by the Hecke operators $T_q$ with $q\neq p$ prime): \[\mathcal{S}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Lambda}),W_{2k}\otimes \theta_d) \cong S_{2k+2}^{\textup{new}}\left(\Gamma_0(p),\varepsilon^{(p)}_p\varepsilon^{(p)}_d\right).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first pick a basis of $\Lambda_p$ realising the diagonal Gram matrix given in the table above and then apply $\hat{\psi}_{(p)}$. This gives us an even lattice $\Pi = V\cap \hat{\psi}_{(p)}(\widehat{\Lambda})$ of discriminant $2p^4$, which we may view as an even lattice of discriminant $2p$ in $(V,Q^{\left(\frac{1}{p}\right)})$ with local lattices: \[\Pi_q \sim\begin{cases} \langle p^{-1}, p^{-1}, 2p^{-1}\rangle \sim \langle 1,1,2p\rangle & \text{ if } q \nmid 2p\\ \left\langle \begin{pmatrix}0 & p^{-1}\\ p^{-1} & 0\end{pmatrix}, -2p^{-1}\right\rangle \sim  \left\langle\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}, -2p\right\rangle & \text{ if } q = 2\\ \langle 1,r,pr\rangle & \text{ if } q = p\equiv 1 \bmod 8\\ \langle 1,1,pr\rangle & \text{ if } q = p\equiv 3 \bmod 8\\ \langle 1,r,p\rangle & \text{ if } q=p\equiv 5 \bmod 8\\ \langle 1,1,p\rangle & \text{ if } q=p\equiv 7 \bmod 8\end{cases}\]

We have that $O(\widehat{\Lambda}) = O(\widehat{\Pi})$ (since $O(\Lambda_p) = O(\Pi_p)$ by Proposition \ref{p-mod} and $O(\Lambda_q) = O(\Pi_q)$ when $q\neq p$), and both Lemma \ref{samespace} and Lemma \ref{scaling} then imply an equality of Hecke modules: \[\mathcal{S}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Lambda}),W) = \mathcal{S}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Pi}),W)\] for every representation $W$ of $O(V)$.

By the recipe outlined in Subsection \ref{Ternary Lattices and Quaternion orders} we find that the even Clifford algebra of $(V,Q^{(\frac{1}{p})})$ is a definite quaternion algebra $B = \text{Cl}^0(V)$ of discriminant $p$. The order $\mathcal{O} = \text{Cl}^0(\Pi)$ has discriminant $\text{discrd}(\mathcal{O}) = p$ and so is maximal, hence residually unramified everywhere with $\varepsilon_p(\mathcal{O}) = -1$. The result then follows from the results of Hein-Tornaria-Voight (see Theorem \ref{thm: 6.12 in HTV}).
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
We give an example of Theorem \ref{genus1}, performing the computations using the Algebraic Modular Forms package in Magma \cite{magma}. We refer to \cite{hein2016orthogonal} for a more in-depth discussion of the practical computational details.

Let $\Lambda = \mathbb{Z}e_1 \oplus \mathbb{Z}e_2 \oplus \mathbb{Z}e_3\subset V$ be an even lattice with Gram matrix \[T = \begin{pmatrix}
		4 & 1 & -1\\ 
        1 & 28 & 9\\ 
        -1 & 9 & 28
	\end{pmatrix}.\] Here, $\text{disc}(\Lambda) = 2738 = 2 \cdot 37^2$. Computations with $p$-neighbours show that $\text{Cl}(\Lambda) = \{[\Lambda_1], [\Lambda_2]\}$ is of size two. The Hecke operators $T_p$ acting on the $2$-dimensional space of trivial weight orthogonal modular forms $\mathcal{M}(O(V), O(\widehat{\Lambda}), \mathbb{C})$ are given by: \begin{align*}
        T_2= \begin{pmatrix}
				1 & 2\\ 
                1 & 2
			\end{pmatrix},\quad T_3= \begin{pmatrix}
				2 & 2\\ 
                1 & 3
			\end{pmatrix},\quad T_5 = \begin{pmatrix}
				2 & 4\\
                2 & 4
			\end{pmatrix},\quad T_7 = \begin{pmatrix}
				2 & 6\\
                3 & 5
			\end{pmatrix},\quad \dots
        \end{align*}
A quick computation then reveals that the eigenforms and eigenvalues are given by:$$
\begin{tabular}{l l l l l l}
			$v_1 = [1,1]$ & $\gamma_{2} = 3$& $\gamma_{3} = 4$& $\gamma_{5} = 6$& $\gamma_{7} = 8$& $\dots$ \\
			$v_2 = [2,-1]$ &  $\lambda_{2} = 0$&  $\lambda_{3} = 1$&  $\lambda_{5} = 0$&  $\lambda_{7} = -1$& $\dots$
		\end{tabular}$$

Note that the first eigenform is the Eisenstein eigenform with eigenvalues $\lambda_p = p+1$. The other eigenform forms a basis for the $1$-dimensional space $\mathcal{S}(O(V), O(\widehat{\Lambda}), \mathbb{C})$ and has eigenvalues $\lambda_p = a_p$ (for $p \neq 37$), where: 
$$f = \sum_{n\geq 1} a_n q^n = q+q^3-2q^4-q^7-2q^9+3q^{11}-2q^{12}-4q^{13}+ \dots $$
is the $q$-expansion of the unique eigenform in $S_2^{\textup{new}}(\Gamma_0(37),-1)$ (having LMFDB label \href{https://www.lmfdb.org/ModularForm/GL2/Q/holomorphic/37/2/a/b/}{37.2.a.b}).

Note that there exists a newform $f_2\in S_2^{\textup{new}}(\Gamma_0(37),+1)$ with LMFDB label \href{https://www.lmfdb.org/ModularForm/GL2/Q/holomorphic/37/2/a/a/}{37.2.a.a}. In accordance with Theorem \ref{genus1}, we do not see this at trivial weight (but it can be seen if the weight is twisted by $\theta_{37}$). The same scenario presents itself also in higher weights.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
One can roughly interpret the above result as telling us that spaces of orthogonal modular forms coming from Genus $1$ admit no newforms. All of the eigenforms that arise are explained by a genus of smaller discriminant $2p$ and so give rise to modular forms of level $p$ (as opposed to level $p^2$). This analogy is a good one to keep in mind for later, but we note that it is not completely accurate since although the lattices $\Lambda$ and $\Pi$ are different, the level structures $O(\widehat{\Lambda})$ and $O(\widehat{\Pi
})$ are equal (in contrast to the congruence subgroups $\Gamma_0(p^2)$ and $\Gamma_0(p)$ being unequal on the modular side).

label: genus2
title: Theorem
body_md: \label{genus2} Let $\Lambda$ be a lattice representing Genus $2$. Then for each $k\geq 0$ and $d\in\{1,2,p,2p\}$ there exists a Hecke-equivariant isomorphism (for the algebra generated by the Hecke operators $T_q$ with $q\neq 2, p$ prime): \[\mathcal{S}(O(\widehat{\Lambda}),W_{2k}\otimes \theta_d) \cong S_{2k+2}^{p\textup{-new}}\left(\Gamma_0(2p),\varepsilon^{(2p)}_p\varepsilon^{(2p)}_d\right).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We again pick a basis of $\Lambda_p$ realising the diagonal Gram matrix given in the table above and then apply $\hat{\psi}_{(p)}$. This gives us an odd lattice $\Pi = V\cap \hat{\psi}_{(p)}(\widehat{\Lambda})$ of discriminant $2p^4$, which we may view as an odd lattice of discriminant $2p$ in $(V,Q^{\left(\frac{1}{p}\right)})$ with local lattices: \[\Pi_q \sim\begin{cases} \langle p^{-1}, p^{-1}, 2p^{-1}\rangle \sim \langle 1,1,2p\rangle & \text{ if } q \nmid 2p\\ \left\langle p^{-1},-p^{-1},-2p^{-1}\right\rangle \sim  \left\langle p,-p,-2p\right\rangle & \text{ if } q = 2\\ \langle 1,r,pr\rangle & \text{ if } q = p\equiv 1 \bmod 8\\ \langle 1,1,pr\rangle & \text{ if } q = p\equiv 3 \bmod 8\\ \langle 1,r,p\rangle & \text{ if } q=p\equiv 5 \bmod 8\\ \langle 1,1,p\rangle & \text{ if } q=p\equiv 7 \bmod 8\end{cases}\]

We have that $O(\widehat{\Lambda}) = O(\widehat{\Pi})$ (since $O(\Lambda_p) = O(\Pi_p)$ by Proposition \ref{p-mod} and $O(\Lambda_q) = O(\Pi_q)$ when $q\neq p$), and both Lemma \ref{samespace} and Lemma \ref{scaling} then imply an equality of Hecke modules: \[\mathcal{S}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Lambda}),W) = \mathcal{S}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Pi}),W)\] for every representation $W$ of $O(V)$.

Note that we cannot apply the results of Hein-Tornaria-Voight yet, since they require an even lattice (their results implicitly require an integral lattice with respect to the quadratic form $Q$, as opposed to the bilinear form $T$). 

 Scaling the quadratic form by $2$ lets us view $\Pi$ as an even lattice of discriminant $16p$ in $(V,Q^{\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)})$, with local lattice $\Pi_2\sim \langle 2p,-2p,-4p\rangle \sim \langle 2,-2,-4p\rangle$. However, further reductions of the discriminant are possible. The lattice $\Omega = V\cap \hat{\psi}_{(2)}(\widehat{\Pi})$ is an even lattice of discriminant $4p$ in $(V,Q^{\left(\frac{2}{p}\right)})$, with local lattices \begin{align*}\Omega_q\sim\begin{cases} \langle2,2,4p\rangle \sim \langle 1,1,p\rangle\qquad & \text{ if } q\nmid 2p\\ 
\left\langle \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix},-4p\right\rangle & \text{ if } q = 2\\ \langle 2,2r,2pr\rangle\sim \langle 1,r,pr\rangle &\text{ if } p\equiv 1 \bmod 8\\ \langle 2,2,2pr\rangle
    \sim \langle 1,1,p\rangle &\text{ if } p\equiv 3 \bmod 8\\
    \langle 2,4,2p\rangle\sim\langle 1,2,2p\rangle &\text{ if } p\equiv 5 \bmod 8\\
    \langle 2,2,2p\rangle \sim \langle 1,1,p\rangle &\text{ if } p\equiv 7 \bmod 8\\
\end{cases}\end{align*}
 
We have that $O(\widehat{\Omega}) = O(\widehat{\Pi})$ (since $O(\Omega_2) = O(\Pi_2)$ by Proposition \ref{4-mod} and $\Pi_q = \Omega_q$ when $q\neq 2$). Another application of Lemma \ref{samespace} and Lemma \ref{scaling} now implies that there is an equality of Hecke modules: \[\mathcal{S}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Pi}),W) = \mathcal{S}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Omega}),W)\] for every representation $W$ of $O(V)$.

By the recipe outlined in Subsection \ref{Ternary Lattices and Quaternion orders} we find that the even Clifford algebra of $(V,Q^{(\frac{2}{p})})$ is a definite quaternion algebra $B = \text{Cl}^0(V)$ of discriminant $p$. The order $\mathcal{O} = \text{Cl}^0(\Omega)$ has discriminant $\text{discrd}(\mathcal{O}) = 2p$ and so is Eichler, hence residually unramified everywhere with $\varepsilon_2(\mathcal{O}) = 1$ and $\varepsilon_p(\mathcal{O}) = -1$. The result then follows from the results of Hein-Tornaria-Voight (see Theorem \ref{thm: 6.12 in HTV}).

title: Example
body_md:
We provide an example in non-trivial weight. Let $\Lambda\subset V$ be an odd lattice with Gram matrix \[T = \begin{pmatrix}
		2 & 0 & 0\\ 
        0 & 11 & 0\\ 
        0 & 0 & 11
	\end{pmatrix}.\]
    One can easily check that $\Lambda$ is a representative for Genus $2$ and that it has discriminant $\text{disc}(\Lambda) = 242 = 2 \cdot 11^2$.
    
    At weight $W_8$ we compute that $\text{dim}(\mathcal{S}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Lambda}),W_8)) = 7$, and the characteristic polynomials of $T_p$ (for $p\neq 11$) have irreducible factors $F_{p,1}(x)$ and $F_{p,2}(x)$ as follows: 

\begin{align*}
    F_{2,1}(x) &= x^5 - 16x^4 - 1506x^3 + 6428x^2 + 619552x + 4247232\\ F_{2,2}(x) &= (x + 16)^2\\ F_{3,1}(x) &= x^5 - 112x^4 - 80330x^3 + 6248892x^2 + 1106354961x + 6873235452\\ F_{3,2}(x) &= x^2 + 21x - 17892\\ F_{5,1}(x) &= x^5 - 1594x^4 - 6694866x^3 + 8153795144x^2 + 11912315141065x - 8650710939654150\\ F_{5,2}(x) &= x^2 + 521x - 2023290\\ &\vdots
\end{align*}

We match these with Galois orbits of newforms $f \in S_{10}^{\text{new}}(\Gamma_0(11))$ and $g \in S_{10}^{\text{new}}(\Gamma_0(22))$ respectively (with LMFDB labels \href{https://www.lmfdb.org/ModularForm/GL2/Q/holomorphic/11/10/a/b/}{11.10.a.b} and \href{https://www.lmfdb.org/ModularForm/GL2/Q/holomorphic/22/10/a/d/}{22.10.a.d}). These forms are both $11$-new and have Atkin-Lehner eigenvalues $-1$ at $11$ and in the second case $+1$ at $2$ (as predicted by Theorem \ref{genus2}). Note that there exist other newforms of levels $11$ and $22$ but they have incorrect Atkin-Lehner eigenvalues, hence we do not see them in this calculation (but we would if we twisted the weight by the characters $\theta_2,\theta_{11}$ and $\theta_{22}$).

title: Example
body_md:
Let $\Lambda$ be a lattice representing Genus $4$ with Gram matrix
\[T = \begin{pmatrix}
        1 & 0 & 0\\
        0 & 2 & 0\\
        0 & 0 & 121
    \end{pmatrix},\]
so that $\text{disc}(\Lambda) = 242 = 2\cdot 11^2$. The class set is trivial, and at weight $W_4$ we compute
$\dim(\mathcal{S}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Lambda}),W_4)\big) = 45$. The characteristic polynomials of $T_3$, $T_5$ and $T_7$ split in the following way and match Galois orbits of newforms (for forms of dimension at least $3$ we only give the degree of the factor):
\[
\renewcommand{1.15}{1.15}
\begin{array}{l|l|l|l|c}

\begin{align*}

\end{align*}
The factors $F_{q,i}$ can be matched with Galois orbits of newforms with respective LMFDB symbols
    \href{https://www.lmfdb.org/ModularForm/GL2/Q/holomorphic/2/10/a/a/}{2.10.a.a},
    \href{https://www.lmfdb.org/ModularForm/GL2/Q/holomorphic/4/10/a/a/}{4.10.a.a},
    \href{https://www.lmfdb.org/ModularForm/GL2/Q/holomorphic/50/10/a/d/}{50.10.a.d},

    \href{https://www.lmfdb.org/ModularForm/GL2/Q/holomorphic/100/10/a/c/}{100.10.a.c} and

\href{https://www.lmfdb.org/ModularForm/GL2/Q/holomorphic/10/10/a/c/}{10.10.a.c} and

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{genusA}
    Let $\Lambda$ be a lattice representing Genus \textup{A}. Then for each $k\geq 0$ and $d\in\{1,2\}$ there exists a Hecke-equivariant isomorphism (for the algebra generated by the Hecke operators $T_q$ with $q\neq 2$ prime): \[\mathcal{S}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Lambda}),W_{2k}\otimes \theta_d) \cong S_{2k+2}^{\textup{new}}\left(\Gamma_0(2),\varepsilon^{(2)}_2\varepsilon^{(2)}_d\right).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Pick a basis of $\Lambda_2$ realising the diagonal Gram matrix given in the table above. We view $\Lambda$ as an odd lattice of determinant $1$ in $(V,Q^{(\frac{1}{2})})$ with local lattice $\Lambda_2 \sim \langle 1,1,1\rangle$. Then the lattice $\Pi = V\cap \hat{\eta}_{(2)}(\widehat{\Lambda})$ is an even lattice of discriminant $4$ with local lattices: \[\Pi_q\sim \begin{cases}\langle 2^{-1},2^{-1},1\rangle \sim \langle 1,1,1\rangle & \text{ if } q \neq 2\\ \left\langle\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}, 12\right\rangle & \text{ if } q = 2\end{cases}\]

We have that $O(\widehat{\Lambda}) = O(\widehat{\Pi})$ (since $O(\Lambda_2) = O(\Pi_2)$ by Proposition \ref{2-unimod} and $\Lambda_q = \Pi_q$ when $q\neq 2$). Another application of Lemma \ref{samespace} and Lemma \ref{scaling} now implies that there is an equality of Hecke modules: \[\mathcal{S}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Lambda}),W) = \mathcal{S}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Pi}),W)\] for every representation $W$ of $O(V)$.

By the recipe outlined in Subsection \ref{Ternary Lattices and Quaternion orders} we find that the even Clifford algebra of $(V,Q^{(\frac{1}{2})})$ is a definite quaternion algebra $B = \text{Cl}^0(V)$ of discriminant $2$. The order $\mathcal{O} = \text{Cl}^0(\Pi)$ has discriminant $\text{discrd}(\mathcal{O}) = 2$ and so is maximal, hence residually unramified everywhere with $\varepsilon_2(\mathcal{O}) = -1$. The result then follows from the results of Hein-Tornaria-Voight (see Theorem \ref{thm: 6.12 in HTV}).

title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Lattices representing genera $3$A, $4$A and $5$A have local $2$-adic lattice isometric to $\langle 2,2,2\rangle$. Following suit from the proof of Theorem \ref{genusA}, we first view $\Lambda$ as an odd lattice of discriminant $p^2$ in $(V,Q^{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)})$ with local Gram matrix $\Lambda_2\sim\langle 1,1,1\rangle$. We then apply the map $\hat{\eta}_{(2)}\in\text{GL}(\hat{V})$ to get an even lattice $\Pi = V\cap \hat{\eta}_{(2)}(\hat{\Lambda})$ of discriminant $4p^2$ with local $2$-adic lattice isometric to $\Pi_2\sim\left\langle\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix},12\right\rangle$. Proposition \ref{2-unimod} tells us that $O(\Lambda_2) = O(\Pi_2)$, and since $O(\Lambda_p) = O(\Pi_p)$ for all primes $p\neq 2$ we must have that $O(\widehat{\Lambda}) = O(\widehat{\Pi})$. As usual, Lemma \ref{samespace} and Lemma \ref{scaling} give us an equality of Hecke modules: \[\mathcal{S}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Lambda}),W) = \mathcal{S}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Pi}),W)\] for every representation $W$ of $O(V)$.

In the case of Genus $3$A we have local lattice $\Pi_p\sim \langle a,p,pb\rangle$ for some $a,b\in\{1,r\}$ and so may also apply the map $\hat{\psi}_{(p)}$ and scale the quadratic map by $\frac{1}{p}$ to receive an even lattice $\Omega = V\cap\hat{\psi}_{(p)}(\widehat{\Pi})$ of discriminant $4p$ in $(V,Q^{\left(\frac{1}{2p}\right)})$. This lattice satisfies $O(\widehat{\Pi}) = O(\widehat{\Omega})$ (by Proposition \ref{p-mod}). Lemma \ref{samespace} and Lemma \ref{scaling} once again give an equality of Hecke modules (for each representation $W$ of $O(V)$): \[\mathcal{S}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Pi}),W) = \mathcal{S}(O(V),O(\widehat{\Omega}),W).\] By the recipe outlined in Subsection \ref{Ternary Lattices and Quaternion orders} we find that the even Clifford algebra of $(V,Q^{(\frac{1}{2p})})$ is a definite quaternion algebra $B = \text{Cl}^0(V)$ of discriminant $2$. The order $\mathcal{O} = \text{Cl}^0(\Omega)$ has discriminant $\text{discrd}(\mathcal{O}) = 2p$ and so is Eichler, hence residually unramified everywhere with $\varepsilon_2(\mathcal{O}) = -1$ and $\varepsilon_p(\mathcal{O}) = 1$. The result then follows from the results of Hein-Tornaria-Voight (see Theorem \ref{thm: 6.12 in HTV}).

In the case of Genus $4$A and Genus $5$A we are unable to further reduce the discriminant. However, one again uses the recipe in Subsection \ref{Ternary Lattices and Quaternion orders} to see that the quaternion algebra $B = \text{Cl}^0(V)$ corresponding to $(V,Q^{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)})$ has discriminant $\text{disc}(B) = 2$ and that the quaternion order $\mathcal{O} = \text{Cl}^0(\Pi)$ has $\text{discrd}(\mathcal{O}) = 2p^2$. This order is locally maximal at $2$ with $\varepsilon_2(\mathcal{O}) = -1$. We also find that $\mathcal{O}$ is locally Eichler at $p$ in the case of Genus $4$A (with $\varepsilon_p(\mathcal{O}) = 1$), whereas it is not locally Eichler at $p$ in the case of Genus $5$A (but has $\varepsilon_p(\mathcal{O}) = -1$). In either case, the order $\mathcal{O}$ is residually unramified everywhere and so another application of Hein-Tornaria-Voight then provides the results as claimed for these genera.
